# Mittavindakajātaka (Ja 104)

**ID:** Ja 104
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Mittavindakajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mittavindakajātaka* (Ja 104) is a birth-story preserved in the *Ekanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection. Set by the Buddha at Jetavana concerning an unruly monk, the frame story introduces a past life dating to the era of the Buddha Kassapa, duplicating the basic plot of an earlier Mittavindaka narrative [Buddhist Critical Thinking Skills 2013]. In the story, the disobedient protagonist Mittavindaka strikes down his mother, embarks on a merchant voyage, is cast adrift by shipmates, and successively visits crystal, silver, jewel, and gold palaces inhabited by four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two celestial nymphs—echoing the opening verse theme "from four to eight" [Buddhist Critical Thinking Skills 2013; Winternitz 1933]. Driven by insatiable craving, he ultimately reaches an iron city where he mistaken identifies a revolving razor-sharp wheel as a lotus bloom, taking upon his head the excruciating torture of the blade-wheel as retribution for his deeds [Buddhist Critical Thinking Skills 2013; Winternitz 1933].

In modern scholarship, the editio princeps of Ja 104 was notable in the editorial history of the collection: Viggo Fausböll recounted that upon reaching Jātaka 104, he had been reduced to a single corrupt Copenhagen manuscript and was close to abandoning his edition until Léon Feer provided collations from the Paris manuscript [Fausböll 1877].
